Turdus migratorius.habitat: Lawns, gardens, parks and open woodland across North America.
Turdus migratorius.song: A cheerful, liquid carol of short rising and falling phrases, often written as "cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio".
Turdus migratorius.fun_fact: Robins are often among the first birds singing before dawn, and they hunt earthworms largely by sight.

Strix aluco.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks and large gardens across Europe and western Asia.
Strix aluco.song: The male gives a long, quavering hoot; the female answers with a sharp "ke-wick".
Strix aluco.fun_fact: The classic "twit-twoo" is usually two owls calling: one "ke-wick" and another hooting in reply.

Erithacus rubecula.habitat: Woodland, hedgerows, parks and gardens across Europe.
Erithacus rubecula.song: A sweet, wistful warble of varied phrases, sung through autumn and winter as well as spring.
Erithacus rubecula.fun_fact: Both males and females sing to defend winter territories, and robins near street lights often sing at night.

Turdus merula.habitat: Woodland, farmland, parks and gardens across Europe; introduced to Australia and New Zealand.
Turdus merula.song: A slow, rich, fluting song made of relaxed, varied phrases.
Turdus merula.fun_fact: Males often sing from rooftops and treetops at dawn and dusk.

Turdus philomelos.habitat: Woodland, hedgerows, parks and gardens across Europe.
Turdus philomelos.song: Loud, clear phrases, each usually repeated two to four times.
Turdus philomelos.fun_fact: Song thrushes smash snail shells against a favourite stone, called an anvil.

Luscinia megarhynchos.habitat: Dense thickets and woodland undergrowth in Europe, North Africa and western Asia.
Luscinia megarhynchos.song: A rich, varied song with deep "jug-jug" notes and long swelling whistles, often sung at night.
Luscinia megarhynchos.fun_fact: The males heard singing at night are mostly unpaired, singing to attract a mate.

Troglodytes troglodytes.habitat: Woodland undergrowth, hedges and gardens across Europe and parts of Asia.
Troglodytes troglodytes.song: A fast, explosive cascade of trills and warbles.
Troglodytes troglodytes.fun_fact: For its tiny size it is one of the loudest songbirds in Europe.

Cardinalis cardinalis.habitat: Woodland edges, thickets and backyards in eastern North America and Mexico.
Cardinalis cardinalis.song: Loud, clear whistles such as "cheer, cheer, cheer" or "birdie, birdie, birdie".
Cardinalis cardinalis.fun_fact: Unlike many songbirds, female cardinals also sing, sometimes from the nest.

Poecile atricapillus.habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests and backyards across northern North America.
Poecile atricapillus.song: A clear, two-note whistle, "fee-bee", alongside the familiar "chick-a-dee-dee-dee" call.
Poecile atricapillus.fun_fact: Adding more "dee" notes to its call can warn other birds of a more dangerous predator.

Zenaida macroura.habitat: Open country, farmland and towns across North America.
Zenaida macroura.fun_fact: The whistling sound on take-off comes from its wings, not its voice.

Strix varia.habitat: Mature forests and swamps, often near water, in eastern North America and spreading west.
Strix varia.song: A rhythmic hooting often written as "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
Strix varia.fun_fact: Barred owls have dark brown eyes, unlike most North American owls, which have yellow eyes.

Bubo virginianus.habitat: Almost every habitat across the Americas, from forests and deserts to cities.
Bubo virginianus.song: Deep, soft hoots in a steady rhythm, like "hoo-h'HOO-hoo-hoo".
Bubo virginianus.fun_fact: Its "horns" are tufts of feathers, not ears.
